# The return direction, every ordered pair

Run on 2026-08-09 on the Linux test host, against the same three foreign
implementations `vendor_bytes.md` records. That file measures one
direction: a value in, bytes out, compared byte for byte. This one
measures the other: those bytes into a *different* implementation, and
the value that comes back compared against the value that went in.

The distinction is the whole reason the phase exists. A byte comparison
passes a decoder that is wrong in the same way its own encoder is wrong,
and a round trip through one implementation passes such a defect every
time. `docs/specs/zerodds-interop-suite-1.0.md` §4, phase P2.

| | |
|---|---|
| Eclipse Cyclone DDS | `/opt/cyclone`, `idlc` + `dds_stream_normalize` + `dds_stream_read_sample` |
| RTI Connext DDS | 7.7.0, `rtiddsgen -language C` + `PRESTypePlugin_interpretedDeserialize` |
| eProsima Fast DDS | `fastddsgen` + the generated `<T>PubSubType::deserialize` |
| ZeroDDS | `wireprobe-zerodds --in`, reflective over the layout plan |

The harness is `tools/wireprobe/wireprobe-pairwise`. For each case it
produces one payload per writer and hands each payload to every reader,
then compares the reader's values against the case's own `values.json` —
never against another reader's answer, because two implementations wrong
in the same way agree with each other and disagree with the sample.

```
tools/pairwise-run/run.sh --out-dir pairwise-out
```

which drives `wireprobe-pairwise` once per (encoding, byte order) and is
the whole run this file records. The driver was `/root/p2-run/run.sh` on
the test host until it was brought into the repository;
[`docs/interop-harnesses.md`](../../../../docs/interop-harnesses.md) is
the index of every harness that produced a figure in this project.

**Which of these pairs a pipeline can regenerate** is in
[`vendor_roundtrip.rows.tsv`](vendor_roundtrip.rows.tsv) beside this
file — the verdict count per (encoding, byte order, writer, reader,
verdict). `tools/pairwise-run/verify.sh` regenerates it and fails on a
count that moved, and the scheduled `interop-vendor-roundtrip` job runs
that against ZeroDDS, Cyclone and Fast DDS in the pinned `ci-interop`
image.

**That file and the tables below are two different measurements, and
the tables are not sums over it.** The tables are the sixteen-pair host
run described above: 314 cases, RTI included, and — as the paragraph
under the matrix says — one dialect for the whole run, Cyclone's. The
`.tsv` is the nine pairs a pipeline can reach, over the corpus as it
stands today (420 cases), with **no dialect named at all**. Re-recorded
2026-09-09 in the `ci-interop` image; the run before it dated from
2026-08-10.

Between those two dates the default dialect changed. `324e99d9865` moved
`Dialect::default` from `Cyclone` to `Specification`, and with it
`default_extensibility` from `Final` to `Appendable` (XTypes 1.3
§7.3.1.2.1.8): a caller who names nothing now gets what the
specification says, which for an aggregate whose source carries no
extensibility annotation means a DHEADER. Cyclone's `idlc` makes the
same source `final` and reads that DHEADER as the first member — hence
`wrote -1234567, read 8`. So the counts move in opposite directions and
both directions are expected: as a share of its pair's rows,
`zerodds→cyclone` `different` goes 1.2 % → 10.0 %, and
`zerodds→fastdds` goes 7.1 % → 1.0 %.

Measured, not inferred: the same three cases run against the same
Cyclone 11.0.1 answer `same` at `d79cb4e472d` and `different` at
`99b3fda37cb`. Whoever needs Cyclone's answers asks for them by name —
`--dialect cyclone` keeps every one of its settings.

| ordered pairs | regenerated by the pipeline |
|---|---|
| the 9 among ZeroDDS, Cyclone and Fast DDS | yes |
| the 7 involving RTI Connext | **no** — licensed and machine-bound, host only |

A pair counts as verified only when **both** ends ran. A matrix that
treated a pair it could not measure as agreeing would be worse than no
matrix, so `verify.sh` names each unverifiable pair instead.

**The recorded counts are not this document's tables**, and the
difference is a change in the harness, not in any implementation. The
run below passed `--policies cyclone`, which names a dialect; every
foreign probe has since learned to refuse a dialect that is not its own
rather than write these bytes and let the run report a divergence it
never measured. A mixed-implementation run therefore passes no dialect
at all — `--policy none`, now the driver's default — and each probe
answers with its own defaults. Re-running the command above with
`--policies cyclone` today would report `unwritten` for every column but
Cyclone's.

## What the verdicts mean

They are kept apart on purpose, because they are findings of different
weight.

| verdict | what happened |
|---|---|
| `same` | the value came back |
| `different` | a value came back **changed** — the finding this phase is for |
| `uncomparable` | the reader produced something that is not a value of this type at all, such as an enumerator name no enumerator has |
| `unread` | the reader refused the payload, or has no binding for the construct |
| `unwritten` | the writer could not produce the case; says nothing about any reader |

`unread` lumps two things that a later revision should separate: a
deserialiser that rejected a payload, and a code generator that rejected
the IDL before there was a payload to reject. Of the 1368 `unread` rows
under XCDR2 little endian, 176 are `rtiddsgen` or `fastddsgen` refusing
the source and 124 are the C binding having no shape for a `map` or a
`bitset` — neither is a decoder result.

**One ordered pair of sixteen round-trips clean**, and it is ZeroDDS
against itself. **Thirty-five cases of 314 come back unchanged on all
sixteen pairs in all four combinations**, and 39 do under XCDR2 little
endian alone.

That number is not a verdict on any decoder. The writer was configured
in one dialect for the whole run — Cyclone's, which is the probe's
default — and three of the four implementations answer at least one wire
question differently from it. The policy table below is the same
measurement with the writer's dialect varied, and it is the number a
user actually needs.

Three of the four self round-trips are also not clean, and each has a
cause on the *writing* side:

- `rti -> rti` and every other RTI or Cyclone row carrying
  `wide_letter`: `fill.rs` emits a `wchar` as `'\u{e4}'`, which is not a
  C character constant. RTI writes `a4c3` where ZeroDDS writes `e400`,
  and the value read back is U+CEA4. 44 rows.
- `cyclone -> cyclone`: six rows, all `-unannotated`, where `idlc` reads
  the type as final and the sample was framed appendable.
- `fastdds -> fastdds`: four rows in the `map` family.

## What the differences are

Every `different` row falls into one of these. The classification is by
case family and by the member the comparison stopped at.

Over all four combinations.

| cause | rows |
|---|---|
| default extensibility — `-unannotated` cases | 483 |
| `wchar` literal in the C fill emitter | 140 |
| union framing | 135 |
| collection delimiter | 66 |
| member id assignment | 52 |
| `wstring` length | 31 |
| map framing | 16 |
| unclassified | 44 |

### The shape a delimiter disagreement takes on the read side

`vendor_bytes.md` §"Where the vendors disagree" records that RTI writes
no collection delimiter where Cyclone and Fast DDS do. Read back, that
is not a length mismatch — it is the delimiter arriving as the first
element's value. Rows from XCDR2 little endian; the same rows appear in
big endian and none of them in XCDR1, which has no delimiter:

```
array-1d-struct-final   zerodds -> rti   Sample.items[0].a: wrote 1, read 14
array-1d-struct-final   cyclone -> rti   Sample.items[0].a: wrote 1, read 14
array-odd-element       fastdds -> rti   Sample.items[0].a: wrote 1, read 14
array-3d-struct         zerodds -> rti   Sample.block[0][0][0].a: wrote -1, read 31
```

Fourteen is the DHEADER. RTI reports no error, returns a sample of the
right shape, and every member in it is one slot late. This is the class
the phase exists to find and it does not show up in a byte comparison at
all: the bytes are exactly what §7.4.3.5 rule (9) says they should be.

The same divergence read the other way is a length that runs off the
end, which does raise an error — `rti -> fastdds` and `rti -> cyclone`
mostly land in `unread`.

### `@hashid` member ids — two separate divergences, since settled

The run recorded this:

```
annotation-hashid-implicit   zerodds -> cyclone   Sample.alpha: wrote -1234567, read 0
annotation-hashid-implicit   zerodds -> rti       Sample.alpha: wrote -1234567, read 0
annotation-hashid-implicit   zerodds -> fastdds   Sample.alpha: wrote -1234567, read 0
annotation-hashid-implicit   cyclone -> rti       Sample.plain: wrote -2, read 0
annotation-hashid-implicit   rti     -> cyclone   Sample.plain: wrote -2, read 0
annotation-hashid-implicit   rti     -> fastdds   Sample.plain: wrote -2, read 0
annotation-hashid-named      zerodds -> cyclone   Sample.beta: wrote 2147483647, read 0
```

A member written under one id and looked for under another is not found,
so the reader returns the member's default. The rows are two different
faults, and they were measured apart in
`vendor_bytes.md` §7.

**`alpha` and `beta` were ZeroDDS's own defect.** XTypes 1.3
§7.3.1.2.1.1 reads the first four bytes of the MD5 as a *little-endian*
`uint32` before masking; this project read them big-endian. All three
vendors read them the way the clause does, and the clause works two
hashes out by hand as the check. Fixed in
`crates/idl-lower/src/complete.rs::hash_id`. Both cases are now
byte-identical between ZeroDDS, Cyclone and Fast DDS:

```
annotation-hashid-implicit   zerodds  180000002c1743237929edff987bca20ffffff7f997bca20feffffff
annotation-hashid-implicit   cyclone  identical
annotation-hashid-implicit   fastdds  identical
annotation-hashid-implicit   rti      …ffffff7f 00000020 feffffff
```

**`plain` is RTI's, and it remains.** `plain` follows two `@hashid`
members and takes the sequential rule. Cyclone, Fast DDS and ZeroDDS
give it the previous member's id plus one; RTI gives it zero, because a
hashed id does not advance its counter. Both readings are written in
§7.3.1.2.1.1, one sentence apart. One EMHEADER word of these twenty-eight
bytes differs, and that word is the whole of the RTI rows above.
`docs/OPEN-ITEMS.md` carries the question of whether a member-id policy
should be able to reproduce it.

### An `@optional` member in a type that is not `@mutable`

`struct { long a; @optional long b; long c; }` with `b` absent, on the
wire from each of the four as this run measured them:

```
cyclone            7929edff 00000000 feffffff        (12)
rti, fastdds       0c000000 7929edff 00000000 feffffff  (16, delimited)
zerodds            7929edff feffffff                 (8)
```

**The clause settles this and the run agrees with it.** The `00000000`
is not "the slot kept and zero-filled": the first byte is a BOOLEAN
`<is_present>` of zero and the other three are the padding before `c`.
XTypes 1.3 §7.4.3.5.2 rule (20) writes exactly that, and §7.4.1.2 gives
the XCDR1 form — a parameter header with a declared length of zero. The
sentence that used to stand here, "which of the two readings the clause
supports is not settled", was a misread: §7.4.2 is the three-paragraph
introduction to encoding version 2 and says nothing about optional
members, while §7.4.3.5.2 says this in one paragraph.

ZeroDDS omitted the member entirely — eight bytes against twelve, and
not exchangeable with any of the three in either direction. It writes
the marker now; `vendor_bytes.md` §1 carries the run with a present
member beside the absent one, which is what tells the two readings
apart.

This is also the case that found a defect in this project's own reader,
recorded below.

## The policy table

The same run with the ZeroDDS writer's dialect varied, XCDR2 little
endian, whole corpus. `--dialect` sets every wire policy at once to the
answers one peer gives; the reader is configured the same way, because a
peer is configured once and not per direction.

Forty cases, the ones the first pass showed a ZeroDDS-to-vendor
divergence on. A whole-corpus sweep is the nightly job; this subset is
where the answer differs at all, so the shape it shows is the shape.

**Which dialect the ZeroDDS writer needs, per reader.**

| cyclone | cyclone | 26 | 2 | 12 | 0 |
| cyclone | rti | 6 | 4 | 29 | 1 |
| cyclone | fastdds | 8 | 6 | 25 | 1 |
| rti | zerodds | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| rti | cyclone | 6 | 14 | 20 | 0 |
| rti | rti | 24 | 3 | 13 | 0 |
| rti | fastdds | 17 | 4 | 19 | 0 |
| fastdds | zerodds | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| fastdds | cyclone | 9 | 14 | 17 | 0 |
| fastdds | rti | 21 | 3 | 16 | 0 |
| fastdds | fastdds | 21 | 4 | 14 | 0 |
| specification | zerodds | 39 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| specification | cyclone | 9 | 14 | 16 | 0 |
| specification | rti | 19 | 3 | 16 | 1 |
| specification | fastdds | 19 | 4 | 14 | 2 |

**The ZeroDDS reader, per writer.**

| dialect | writer | same | different | unread | uncomparable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cyclone | zerodds | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| cyclone | cyclone | 20 | 0 | 5 | 0 |
| cyclone | rti | 6 | 1 | 19 | 0 |
| cyclone | fastdds | 7 | 0 | 19 | 0 |
| rti | zerodds | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| rti | cyclone | 4 | 0 | 21 | 0 |
| rti | rti | 18 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| rti | fastdds | 13 | 2 | 11 | 0 |
| fastdds | zerodds | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| fastdds | cyclone | 6 | 0 | 18 | 0 |
| fastdds | rti | 15 | 4 | 6 | 0 |
| fastdds | fastdds | 17 | 1 | 7 | 0 |
| specification | zerodds | 39 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| specification | cyclone | 7 | 0 | 17 | 0 |
| specification | rti | 13 | 4 | 8 | 0 |
| specification | fastdds | 15 | 1 | 9 | 0 |

**Set the dialect to the peer.** `--dialect cyclone` reads 26 of 40
through Cyclone and 8 through Fast DDS; `--dialect fastdds` reads 21
through Fast DDS and 9 through Cyclone. On these cases the setting is
worth the difference between interoperating and not, and there is no
setting that is best against all three at once — which is what a policy
table is for.

**`rti` and `fastdds` are close but not the same**, and both differ from
`specification`. The three agree on default extensibility, which is what
most of this subset turns on; they part on the collection delimiter and
on the PL_CDR1 header form, which shows in the `rti`-versus-`fastdds`
rows against Fast DDS.

**The ZeroDDS reader returns a changed value in eight rows of 160**, all
of them in three groups, and the groups are worth naming because two of
the three are not the reader's fault:

- `array-1d-primitives` and its twin, writer RTI: the bytes really do
  hold U+CEA4, because `fill.rs` emits a `wchar` as `'\u{e4}'`, which is
  not a C character constant. The reader reported what was there.
- `annotation-must-understand-unannotated`, writer RTI: an `@optional
  @must_understand string` came back absent.
- `annotation-optional-absent-unannotated`, writers RTI and Fast DDS:
  `c` came back 0.

The last two were one defect in this project's reader, and the pairwise
run is what found it. See below.

## The defect this run found in our own reader

Taking an `@optional` member as absent was a guess: this project read
the next four bytes as a member header and, when the id was not the one
it expected, concluded the member had not been written.

Against a stream that marks the gap the guess is wrong, and it was wrong
*quietly*. The reader took the `<is_present>` byte and its padding for a
header that did not match, called `b` absent, read `c` out of those same
four bytes as 0, and the delimiter swallowed the four real bytes of `c`
as if they were an appendable tail from a newer writer. A sample of the
right shape, one member holding the wrong value, no error anywhere.

Making the guess falsifiable against the delimiter turned that into a
refusal. Writing and reading the marker removes the guess: rule (20) and
§7.4.1.2 say what is there, all three implementations write it, and the
reader now reads a value again. The speculative header read, the
`guessed` list, the delimiter-remainder check and the C column's
mark-and-rewind around it are gone with it — the one reader mark left in
the generated C is the `map` counting pass under `rule-15-omits`, which
is a genuine two-pass read.

`crates/wire-probe/tests/decode_round_trip.rs`,
`the_optional_marker_is_the_one_the_vendors_write_and_read`, holds the
three implementations' bytes for a present and an absent member in both
encoding versions and asserts this project produces them and reads
them.

## The four combinations side by side

| encoding | byte order | same | different | unread | unwritten | uncomparable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| xcdr2 | le | 2210 | 338 | 1368 | 1096 | 12 |
| xcdr2 | be | 2200 | 347 | 1378 | 1088 | 11 |
| xcdr1 | le | 3140 | 137 | 647 | 1096 | 4 |
| xcdr1 | be | 3126 | 145 | 661 | 1088 | 4 |

**XCDR1 interoperates far better than XCDR2**: 3140 rows the same against
2210, and 137 changed values against 338. The reason is the delimiter.
XCDR1 has no delimited encoding, so `@appendable` and `@final` are the
same bytes and the default-extensibility divergence — 186 of the 338
XCDR2 differences — cannot arise. Two thirds of what separates these four
implementations under XCDR2 is a header XCDR1 does not have.

Big endian is the same measurement to within ten rows in every column,
which is what `vendor_bytes.md` §"What the byte order changes, and what
it does not" already reported from the write side: nothing but the byte
order. Where the four agree in little endian they agree in big endian,
and where they split they split into the same groups.

All four ran to completion. The harness is
[`tools/pairwise-run/`](../../../../tools/pairwise-run/) and the reports
are what `--out-dir` leaves behind; a whole-corpus dialect sweep, of
which the forty-case table above is the part that differs, was still
running.

## Reproducing

From a checkout, with whichever vendors are installed:

```
cargo build -p zerodds-wire-probe --bins
tools/pairwise-run/run.sh --out-dir pairwise-out       # every combination
tools/pairwise-run/verify.sh --impls zerodds,cyclone,fastdds
```

Sixteen seconds for the binaries on the test host — `wire-probe`'s
dependency closure is nine crates. A vendor that is not installed is
named with the rows it costs and the run continues.

`WIREPROBE_CACHE` is what makes it affordable: the sixteen decode runs
of one case differ only in the payload on stdin, and regenerating
through `fastddsgen` for each of them spends the whole budget on the
code generator. With the cache warm the whole corpus in one encoding and
byte order is about ten minutes on eight cores; without it, hours.

One case, one pair, by hand:

```
tools/wireprobe/wireprobe-rti --idl <case>/type.idl --type Sample \
    --values <case>/values.json --encoding xcdr2 --endian le --out rti.bin
tools/wireprobe/wireprobe-cyclone --idl <case>/type.idl --type Sample \
    --in rti.bin --encoding xcdr2 --endian le --values-out read.json
target/debug/wireprobe-compare --idl <case>/type.idl --type Sample \
    --expected <case>/values.json --found read.json
```
